title: INTERVIEW: Shipping Perfectly Placed For Green Fuel Markets But Broader Adoption Needed First
description:
Torben Nørgaard, vice president and head of partnerships and offtake in power-to-X at European Energy.
European Energy operates Kassø in southern Denmark, the world's first commercial-scale e-methanol plant.
In contrast, Nørgaard sees Shipping having lost the leading position on green fuel regulation it held only a few years ago.
"The wind didn't start blowing because the shipping industry built wind-propulsion ships," he quipped.
And despite the missed opportunities related to shipping regulation, Nørgaard believes the industry's orderbook shows it is instinctively returning to what it does best: keeping its options open.
text:
Torben Nørgaard, vice president and head of partnerships and offtake in power-to-X at European Energy. Image Credit: European Energy

As demand for green fuels grows across transport and industry, European Energy's Torben Nørgaard sees an opportunity for shipping to tap into a much larger and more mature market

Kassø e-methanol plant sells every droplet it can produce, with German land transport now driving demand

Shipping has been "overtaken" on e-fuels after missed opportunities but has potential to regain momentum under EU and global regulation

From sail to coal to diesel to LNG, shipping has always run on fuels other industries made available

Shipping is not well structured to create the markets for the green fuels it needs to achieve its goal to decarbonize, but is in a perfect position to play in them once others have built them, according to Torben Nørgaard, vice president and head of partnerships and offtake in power-to-X at European Energy.

"They are structurally challenged to create the markets, but they're in a perfect place to play in the markets, because actually they benefit from being very flexible in the approach to how they choose fuels," he told Ship & Bunker in an interview this week.

Nørgaard has seen the question from both sides. Before joining the Danish renewables developer he spent five years as chief technology officer of the Maersk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping (MMMCZCS), following a career building methanol, ammonia, and hydrogen plants with Topsøe and 15 years in oil and gas.

Overtaken at Its Own Game

Nørgaard's view carries particular weight because of where he now sits. European Energy operates Kassø in southern Denmark, the world's first commercial-scale e-methanol plant.

The 52 MW facility has a nameplate capacity of 42,000 mt/year, has been producing for around one and a half years, and counts Maersk, Novo Nordisk, and LEGO as its founding offtakers.

"The plant is running at full capacity, and we sell every droplet we can produce," Nørgaard said.

"Demand currently exceeds the volumes we are able to produce. At Kassø, we are capacity constrained rather than customer constrained."

Kassø demonstrates that the market for e-methanol is no longer hypothetical. The question is increasingly how quickly supply can scale as regulation spurs uptake across multiple sectors.

Demand is increasingly broadening beyond shipping, with regulation now creating new markets for renewable fuels of non-biological origin (RFNBO) in European road transport and industry, thanks to drivers that include Germany's adoption of a 0.1% blending mandate for RFNBO fuels in gasoline from January 1 this year.

Meeting that mandate for Germany alone requires around 150,000 mt/year of RFNBO-compliant methanol, Nørgaard said, with RFNBO non-compliance penalties equivalent to roughly €2,400 per tonne of methanol to be added to the regular emission compliance, setting an effective price point in an undersupplied market.

The blending level is set to rise towards 5-10% over the next decade, he said, with the mandate spreading to other European countries and to industries such as steel.

In contrast, Nørgaard sees Shipping having lost the leading position on green fuel regulation it held only a few years ago.

Indeed, Shipping was set to become the first industry with a global, legally binding net-zero framework, only for agreement on the proposed scheme to collapse at last October's extraordinary MEPC session.

"Shipping was among the first sectors to create regulatory momentum around green fuels. Other sectors are now moving quickly as well, which can ultimately help build the scale and liquidity that shipping needs," he said.

A proposed auctioning mechanism for RFNBO-compliant fuel under FuelEU Maritime "could be a bit of a game-changer, subject to how it's implemented," he added.

Why Shipping is Challenged to Be the Market Maker

For Nørgaard, the industry's familiar "chicken and egg" framing, where owners wait for fuel supply certainty while producers wait for demand certainty, misses the real problem.

A functioning market needs traded volumes, liquidity, and depth, he argues, and a new one needs a market maker prepared to stand behind it for five to ten years.

"Creating a new global fuel market requires long-term commitments, liquidity and substantial investment across the value chain. That is difficult for any fragmented global industry to deliver on its own," he said.

"That is why regulation and demand from several sectors are so important. They allow producers to scale supply while giving shipping greater flexibility over how and when it adopts new fuels." Energy systems, he says, are built by nation states and regions to serve many industries at once, almost never by a single sector acting alone.

The Way It Has Always Worked

If that sounds like a demotion for shipping, Nørgaard's point is that running on energy systems built by others is exactly what the industry has done throughout its history.

"The wind didn't start blowing because the shipping industry built wind-propulsion ships," he quipped.

"They didn't shift to coal because someone invented a coal ship and thereby created demand for coal; they went there because the coal industry was developed by other sectors and was made available on a spot basis. Same story on diesel."

LNG followed the same pattern, he said. Its supply chain was built to give power generators in Japan and Korea security of energy supply, and ships operating on those routes simply tapped into it.

On that view, heavy fuel oil is the historical exception rather than the rule, a leftover product few other industries wanted.

Room for Everything

That flexibility is also why Nørgaard is relaxed about the prospect of surplus bioethanol entering the marine fuel market as electric vehicles eat into road demand, a shift that could free up 5-10 million mt for other uses including shipping.

Bioethanol delivers anywhere from close to none to 70% carbon reductions depending on how it is produced, he said, placing it in a different category from e-methanol's deep emission reduction potential rather than in direct competition with it.

"I think we should embrace and welcome bioethanol to the marketplace," he said. "Different fuels will play different roles. E-methanol offers a pathway to very deep emissions reductions and can be produced at scale using renewable electricity and biogenic CO₂."

As for where European Energy builds next, the fundamentals are access to biogenic CO₂, low-cost renewable electricity, land and, increasingly, access to markets created by regulation.

"Kassø has given us practical experience of what it takes to develop, build and operate e-methanol production at commercial scale. For future projects, the fundamentals are clear to us," he said, while stressing the company has nothing public to announce.

And despite the missed opportunities related to shipping regulation, Nørgaard believes the industry's orderbook shows it is instinctively returning to what it does best: keeping its options open.

"They're doing the right thing, if you ask me," he said.

"Shipping is building optionality into the fleet and positioning itself to use the fuels that become available at scale. The next step is creating regulatory frameworks that allow shipping to compete with road transport and industry for low-emission fuels. If we get that right, demand from multiple sectors can help bring the scale that ultimately makes these fuels more accessible to everyone."

text:
TOKYO: The Global Ro-Ro Community (GRC)*1, whose participants include Ro-Ro carriers and other stakeholders, and which covers approximately 80% of the transport capacity of the global car carrier fleet*2, has established the GRC Council (GRCC), a body responsible for the operation of the GRC. Since the establishment of the GRC, ClassNK has participated as an independent verifier. In connection with the establishment of the GRCC, ClassNK has also contributed to the development of its operational foundation through the formulation of the Governance Framework and data handling rules.

With the establishment of the GRCC, a formal governance framework has been put in place for the continuous review and improvement of emissions accounting methodologies and data handling rules. This will strengthen the environment in which not only Ro-Ro carriers, but also cargo owners and vehicle manufacturers, can utilize reliable and transparent GHG emissions data. As a result, emissions management and decarbonization efforts throughout the supply chain can be advanced more effectively. In addition, the continuous improvement of internationally aligned emissions accounting methodologies is expected to enhance the transparency of environmental information and promote decarbonization across the industry.

ClassNK will continue to support decarbonization efforts of shipping companies, cargo owners, vehicle manufacturers, and other stakeholders through the promotion of emissions accounting based on reliable primary data, drawing on its expertise and experience as an independent verifier.

Background to the Establishment of the GRCC

Growing demand for reliable primary emissions data is being driven by developments such as FuelEU Maritime, the IMO’s greenhouse gas reduction measures, and the advancement of corporate Scope 3 emissions disclosure requirements. Against this background, the GRC was established in 2024 to promote cross-industry collaboration between Ro-Ro carriers and cargo owners. The GRC brings together Ro-Ro carriers, independent verifiers, cargo owners and other stakeholders to improve the accuracy, transparency and comparability of greenhouse gas emissions accounting. Participating companies account for approximately 80% of the transport capacity of the global car carrier fleet and are working to establish an industry-wide emissions data platform.

As these activities have expanded, the maintenance and improvement of the methodology, the management of data handling rules, and the transparency of decision-making processes have become increasingly important challenges. As a self-governing organization of carriers and verifiers, the GRCC is responsible for the ongoing review and enhancement of the GRC Methodology*3, data handling rules and related governance documents. Through these efforts, the GRCC is expected to contribute to carriers’ communication of environmental performance and to support more effective Scope 3 emissions management and enhanced decarbonization strategies such as by cargo owners and vehicle manufacturers, while also improving the transparency of environmental information throughout the supply chain.

ClassNK’s Role

Since the establishment of the GRC, ClassNK has served as an independent verifier and provides verification services for GHG emissions data in accordance with the GRC Methodology. By supporting transparent and consistent emissions accounting based on verified primary data, ClassNK contributes to the development of a trusted emissions data foundation for the Ro-Ro sector.

In preparation for the establishment of the GRCC, ClassNK participated in the development of the GRC Governance Framework and data handling rules and supported the preparation of related maritime legal documentation.

Furthermore, Mr. Hiroshi Ochi, General Manager, Green Certification Department, ClassNK has been elected Vice-Chair of the GRCC, among other contributions made by ClassNK toward the establishment and operation of the new governance framework.

*1 A programme established by Smart Freight Centre (SFC), an international non-profit organization dedicated to reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in the logistics sector. The GRC brings together Ro-Ro carriers, independent verifiers, cargo owners and other stakeholders to improve the accuracy, transparency and comparability of greenhouse gas emissions accounting.

*2 Based on Car Equivalent Units (CEU)

*3 A GHG emissions accounting methodology for Ro-Ro shipping published by the GRC in 2025. The methodology is aligned with ISO 14083 and the GLEC Framework and enables the calculation of vessel-level GHG emission intensity factors based on independently verified primary data.

text:
Biomethane could cover 70% of shipping’s early IMO fuel demand

In Denmark, the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping projects global biomethane supply could reach 21 billion cubic meters by 2030 under its base case, enough in theory to cover about 70% of the low emissions fuel demand created by the proposed IMO Net-Zero Framework. A stronger policy driven scenario could lift supply to 52 billion cubic meters.

The center estimates the IMO framework could generate unconstrained demand equivalent to 29.7 billion cubic meters of biomethane in 2030. Actual use would be lower because only methane capable vessels can consume the fuel, and shipping would compete with other sectors for supply.

The analysis identifies mass balance accounting as a key condition for scaling marine biomethane. Allowing certified biomethane injected into gas grids to be credited to ships bunkering elsewhere would let the industry use existing LNG infrastructure instead of building physically segregated supply chains.

The center said biomethane could become one of shipping’s few scalable near term compliance options if the IMO recognizes a credible global mass balance system.

text:
The organisation plans to advance work on global regulation, insurance and liability, and port readiness this year, managing director Virginia Crosbie told classification society RINA.

It also aims to publish a practical guide covering insurability and port governance for commercial vessels by 2027.

NEMO was granted non-governmental consultative status at the IMO last year and plans to work with the IMO, Nuclear Energy Agency, International Atomic Energy Agency and classification societies to develop the frameworks needed for commercial deployment.

Nuclear power could initially be suited to fixed routes and ice-class vessels, as well as “energy intensive offshore activities”, Crosbie said.

“Over the longer term, if regulatory clarity and financing confidence mature, nuclear could become a scalable pillar for parts of the [large ocean going] fleet where high energy density and endurance are decisive advantages,” she added.

The development of small modular reactor technology could also enable nuclear power to be used for shore power and green fuel production, according to Crosbie.

Several NEMO members are already exploring maritime nuclear applications.

text:
India plans to mandate E10 fuel for coastal trade vessels starting in 2029 to accelerate green shipping and lower maritime carbon emissions.

New Delhi: Aiming to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from the maritime sector, the Central Government has released a draft roadmap for promoting the progressive adoption of low-carbon and renewable marine fuels. The initiative aligns with the National Maritime Decarbonisation Policy Framework (NMDPF), the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018, and India’s broader climate objectives. A document released by the Directorate General of Marine Administration (DGMA) noted that biofuels and their blends provide an immediate, practical pathway to cut emissions without major shipboard modifications.

What is Directorate General of Marine Administration planning on Biofuels?

“Biofuels, particularly suitable drop-in biofuels and their blends with conventional marine fuels, provide an immediate and practical pathway for reducing lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions associated with marine transportation without requiring substantial modifications to existing shipboard fuel systems,” a document released by the Directorate General of Marine Administration (DGMA) on Wednesday says.

In order to provide a predictable transition pathway for the maritime industry, promote the availability of sustainable marine biofuels and progressively reduce the carbon intensity of vessels operating in Indian coastal waters, the DGMA has decided to introduce a phased framework for the use of biofuel blends in marine fuels, it says.

“The requirements of this Notice shall apply to vessels using the following conventional marine fuels: Marine Gas Oil (MGO); Very Low Sulphur Fuel Oil (VLSFO); and Fuel Oil (FO), including applicable residual marine fuel grades used for propulsion or auxiliary machinery.

The requirements shall apply, as applicable, to shipowners, ship managers, operators, charterers, masters, bunker suppliers, fuel producers/blenders and other stakeholders involved in the procurement, blending, supply, bunkering and use of marine fuel by vessels engaged in Coastal Trade,” the document says.

10% Biofuel Blend plan

According to it, a biofuel is a fuel oil which is derived from biomass and hence includes, but is not limited to, processed used cooking oils, fatty-acid-methyl-esters (FAME) or fatty-acid-ethylesters (FAEE), straight vegetable oils (SVO), hydro-treated vegetable oils (HVO), glycerol or other biomass-to-liquid (BTL) type products. The DGMA has proposed a “10% Biofuel Blend”.

With effect from January 1, 2029, every vessel covered under the notice and engaged in Indian coastal trade shall use, for propulsion and auxiliary machinery, marine fuel containing not less than 10% biofuel by volume when operating under coastal trade, subject to the provisions relating to exemptions and exceptional circumstances contained in this notice, the DGMA says.

Kolkata, Aug 19 (SocialNews.XYZ) Aiming at reducing greenhouse gas emissions from the maritime sector, the Central Government has released a draft roadmap for promoting the progressive adoption of low-carbon and renewable marine fuels in line with the National Maritime Decarbonisation Policy Framework (NMDPF), the National Policy on Biofuels, 2018, and India’s broader maritime decarbonisation objectives.

"Biofuels, particularly suitable drop-in biofuels and their blends with conventional marine fuels, provide an immediate and practical pathway for reducing lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions associated with marine transportation without requiring substantial modifications to existing shipboard fuel systems," a document released by the Directorate General of Marine Administration (DGMA) on Wednesday says.

In order to provide a predictable transition pathway for the maritime industry, promote the availability of sustainable marine biofuels and progressively reduce the carbon intensity of vessels operating in Indian coastal waters, the DGMA has decided to introduce a phased framework for the use of biofuel blends in marine fuels, it says.

The objective is to promote the use of renewable and lower-carbon marine fuels; reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions from coastal shipping; develop and strengthen domestic production, supply and bunkering infrastructure for sustainable marine biofuels; facilitate a smooth transition towards low- and zero-carbon marine fuels; and support implementation of the National Maritime Decarbonisation Policy Framework.

The order to use blended fuel shall apply to all vessels engaged in Indian Coastal Trade, irrespective of flag, which are required to obtain or operate under a licence or permission for engagement in the coastal trade of India.

"The requirements of this Notice shall apply to vessels using the following conventional marine fuels: Marine Gas Oil (MGO); Very Low Sulphur Fuel Oil (VLSFO); and Fuel Oil (FO), including applicable residual marine fuel grades used for propulsion or auxiliary machinery. The requirements shall apply, as applicable, to shipowners, ship managers, operators, charterers, masters, bunker suppliers, fuel producers/blenders and other stakeholders involved in the procurement, blending, supply, bunkering and use of marine fuel by vessels engaged in Coastal Trade," the document says.

According to it, a biofuel is a fuel oil which is derived from biomass and hence includes, but is not limited to, processed used cooking oils, fatty-acid-methyl-esters (FAME) or fatty-acid-ethylesters (FAEE), straight vegetable oils (SVO), hydro-treated vegetable oils (HVO), glycerol or other biomass-to-liquid (BTL) type products.

The DGMA has proposed a “10% Biofuel Blend”. This means that homogeneous marine fuel should contain not less than 10% biofuel by volume. It has explained that “sustainable biofuel” means biofuel produced from eligible feedstock through a recognised or approved production pathway and supported by appropriate sustainability documentation or certification demonstrating its origin, traceability and lifecycle greenhouse gas characteristics.

"With effect from January 1, 2028, all vessels engaged in Indian Coastal Trade are encouraged to use biofuel blends containing up to 10% biofuel by volume with MGO, VLSFO or FO, as applicable, subject to fuel availability, compatibility, safety, engine/equipment manufacturer’s recommendations and compliance with applicable statutory requirements. During this period, shipowners/operators/charterers should progressively establish arrangements for procurement of compliant biofuel blends; fuel compatibility and stability assessment; onboard fuel management and storage arrangements; crew familiarisation and training; monitoring of fuel consumption and machinery performance; and maintenance of appropriate records for demonstrating the use of biofuel blends," it has said.

With effect from January 1, 2029, every vessel covered under the notice and engaged in Indian coastal trade shall use, for propulsion and auxiliary machinery, marine fuel containing not less than 10% biofuel by volume when operating under coastal trade, subject to the provisions relating to exemptions and exceptional circumstances contained in this notice, the DGMA says.

While vessels will have to arrange for additional tanks to carry biofuel, a ship shall not be considered compliant merely by carrying biofuel separately onboard without blending it with the applicable conventional marine fuel, unless specifically permitted by the Directorate under an approved alternative compliance arrangement.

text:
Infrastructure, certification and regulation could limit the amount of biomethane that reaches shipping, rather than feedstock availability, according to Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping (MMMCZCS).

IMAGE: A large container cargo ship sailing. Getty Images

Global biomethane supply could reach around 21 billion cubic metres (bcm) by 2030 under a base-case scenario, per MMMCZCS.

The volume could theoretically cover around 70% of the low-emissions fuel demand that the IMO's proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF) could create in 2030.

The centre estimates this demand would be equivalent to around 29.7 billion cubic meters (bcm) of biomethane, if biomethane were to meet it entirely.

A faster, policy-driven growth scenario could lift biomethane supply to around 52 bcm by 2030, above the estimated NZF-induced requirement.

However, the actual amount that shipping can use could be lower.

MMMCZCS estimates that if all methane-fuelled container vessels used liquefied biomethane (LBM), shipping could absorb around 11 million tonnes of LSFO-equivalent biomethane by 2030.

That would represent around 56% of the projected 21 bcm base-case supply.

A key enabler for shipping to access this supply is mass balancing, which allows biomethane injected into the natural gas grid to be credited to maritime fuel use elsewhere through a certified chain of custody.

Without a globally recognised system, shipping would have to rely on physically segregated biomethane supply chains, which MMMCZCS said would be difficult and costly to scale.

The centre said shipping's ability to use biomethane will also depend on the growth of the methane-capable fleet and bunkering infrastructure.

Biomethane can only be used by ships capable of burning methane-based fuels, while bunker barges and terminal capacity would also need to expand.

Additionally, shipping will also compete with other sectors for the same supply, and stronger demand from other users could limit the amount available to the maritime industry.

text:
The Clean Shipping Alliance (CSA) and the Marine Fuels Alliance (MFA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to support the shipping industry and bunker suppliers in meeting regulatory requirements on emissions, and to advance the transition to alternative fuels and emissions reduction technologies.

The agreement will see CSA's expertise in exhaust gas cleaning systems and marine environmental technology brought together with MFA's network and knowledge across the marine fuels supply chain. Both organizations share an interest in supporting the maritime industry's transition toward a sustainable, compliant and lower-emission future, and the agreement sets out a structure for the two bodies to share technical insight and coordinate on regulatory pathways.

Through the collaboration, the two associations intend to encourage dialogue between technology providers, fuel suppliers and ship operators, share technical insights and support the development of practical regulatory pathways.

Under this framework, the two associations will:

Share technical data and research: on MARPOL compliance, alternative fuels and emissions reduction technologies.

Coordinate joint advocacy: including at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) level and alongside sessions of the IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC).

Support industry events: on fleet modernisation, retrofitting and fuel quality standards.

Develop practical operational guidance: linking technology providers, fuel suppliers and ship operators.

Andreas Chrysostomou, Executive Director of the Clean Shipping Alliance, said: “Shipping's compliance and availability challenges won't be solved by one technology or one fuel. It needs ongoing communication between different elements of the value chain, and that's why CSA and MFA have signed this MoU. Technologies, fuels and regulation cannot be considered in isolation, and by working together we can bring together complementary expertise, improve the exchange of technical knowledge and contribute to solutions that are both environmentally effective and operationally realistic.”

Anthony Mollet, Executive Officer of the Marine Fuels Alliance, said: “The CSA brings a wealth of technical knowledge and first-hand industry experience, particularly in relation to emissions, environmental regulation and the technologies being adopted by shipowners and operators. This partnership will give our members an important additional source of expertise and insight, helping them better understand the challenges facing the industry and make informed decisions as the transition towards cleaner shipping continues.

“For companies across the contractual chain in bunkers, it is increasingly important to understand the decisions being made by shipowners and operators around fuel choice, emissions technologies and the future fuels they intend to use. The selection of a particular fuel grade or technology can have significant implications throughout the bunker supply chain, from contractual arrangements and fuel specifications to supply and operational considerations. text:
This has prompted concerns that shipping-specific greenhouse gas (GHG) regulations could move faster than the availability of lower-emissions fuels needed to meet them.

The analysis examines whether biomethane—a technologically mature energy carrier that is compatible with existing infrastructure—could scale sufficiently to meet regulated demand. The International Maritime Organization’s draft Net-Zero Framework (IMO NZF) is used as a benchmark.

While the framework remains under discussion, it provides a useful proxy for several plausible and increasingly likely regulatory pathways for shipping and other hard-to-abate sectors.

Furthermore, the analysis finds that biomethane could play a significant role in the shipping sector’s early compliance response, provided the necessary regulatory conditions are in place. MMMCZCS estimates that total unconstrained demand for low-emissions fuel resulting from the NZF in 2030 would be equivalent to around 30 billion cubic metres (bcm) of biomethane if the fuel were to meet the entire demand.

Actual uptake would be lower, however, constrained by the size of the methane-capable fleet, bunkering infrastructure and competition for biomethane from other sectors.

Global biomethane supply could reach around 21 bcm by 2030 under a ‘base’ case and as much as 52 bcm under a policy-driven ‘max’ case. Both estimates are well below the global technical potential identified by the International Energy Agency (IEA), suggesting that feedstock availability is unlikely to be the main constraint.

Instead, infrastructure, certification, regulation and access to existing gas and LNG value chains are likely to determine how quickly supply can scale.

In addition, certification will be particularly important. Without internationally recognised mass-balance accounting, shipping would likely need to rely on physically segregated biomethane supply chains, making large-scale deployment significantly more difficult and costly.

Mass-balance systems therefore remain a key hurdle and will require greater regulatory clarity.

Overall, the analysis suggests that biomethane could provide a substantial source of lower-emissions energy for shipping under plausible supply and policy conditions.

However, the sector will be competing with other industries for the same molecules, and stronger willingness to pay elsewhere could limit shipping’s access to biomethane as an abatement option.

Before 2030, the availability of grid-adjacent feedstocks is unlikely to be the binding constraint. The more fundamental question is whether shipping can gain access to the wider gas-based energy system through a credible, internationally recognised and certified mass-balance framework.

As informed, ISO 22120:2026, titled Ships and marine technology — Specification for bunkering of methanol fuelled vessels, was published in August 2026 as the first edition. The standard establishes requirements for methanol bunkering transfer systems and equipment and is intended to provide a consistent international framework for conducting bunkering operations safely.

The standard covers five key areas:

transfer systems,

operational procedures,

risk assessment,

safety protection,

and personnel training.

ISO said the standard was developed in response to an industry need for additional safety guidance for alternative marine fuels, identified by the International Maritime Organization (IMO). It is intended to support the IMO International Code of Safety for Ships using Gases or other Low-flashpoint Fuels (IGF Code) and the IMO Interim Guidelines for the Safety of Ships Using Methyl/Ethyl Alcohol as Fuel.

The document provides requirements covering the equipment and systems used to transfer methanol between shore-based or floating facilities and receiving vessels.

It also addresses safety measures including emergency release systems, emergency shutdown systems, safety zones and procedures for managing methanol transfer operations.

ISO noted that the growing number of methanol-fuelled vessels has been accompanied by an increase in methanol bunkering operations, creating a need for greater international standardization.

The new requirements are intended to give vessel operators a basis for selecting fuel providers that meet defined safety standards and to support safer and more consistent bunkering operations.

This document was prepared by Technical Committee ISO/TC 8, Ships and marine technology, Subcommittee SC 25, Maritime GHG reduction.

text:
Recently, Shanghai Yangshan Port held a green methanol bunkering event. Shanghai Electric, together with Shanghai International Port Group and French CMA CGM Group, completed a batch bunkering of 8,000 mt of green methanol, setting a new world record for the largest single green methanol bunkering volume and marking the project's further progress into the stage of continuous stable production and large-scale delivery.

The green methanol used in this bunkering was supplied by Shanghai Electric's Taonan Green Methanol Project. The new breakthrough in bunkering volume reflects that China's green fuel industry is enhancing its coordination capabilities across production, transportation, storage, and port application, and provides practical support for the shipping industry in expanding the use of low-carbon fuels.

In June this year, Shanghai, Jilin, and Liaoning jointly launched a green fuel transport corridor, creating a complete logistics chain from production in Taonan, Jilin, through transshipment and storage at Dalian Port in Liaoning, to bunkering at Shanghai Port. The successful bunkering of 8,000 mt of green methanol this time marks the first large-scale validation of the corridor since it became operational.

Currently, Shanghai is accelerating the construction of an international shipping green fuel bunkering center, certification center, and trading center. This batch bunkering serves as both a staged demonstration of the construction achievements and a new opportunity to further deepen cooperation between the green fuel supply chain and industry chain.

As the main production site for green methanol, Shanghai Electric's Taonan Project relies on the abundant wind energy and biomass resources in Jilin. It employs a complete set of process systems and core equipment independently developed by Shanghai Electric, including pure-oxygen pressurized fluidized bed biomass gasification technology, to build the world's first large-scale plant coupling green electricity with biomass to produce green methanol.

Currently, the project has entered the stage of continuous stable production and batch delivery, and can continuously supply green methanol products based on the actual needs of vessels at the Shanghai International Shipping Center. The project's stable supply further verifies the full-chain operational capability of green methanol from the production end, through the transportation end, to the port bunkering end.

Looking ahead, Shanghai Electric will continue to strengthen industrial collaboration with partners such as the National Green Development Fund, and promote technological innovation and project construction across the entire chain of green fuel production, storage, transportation, and application. Meanwhile, the company will work with relevant parties to accelerate the construction of the green hydrogen coupled with biomass integrated green methanol-oil project in Taonan, enhancing the large-scale supply capability of green fuels for the shipping and aviation sectors.

This event was jointly completed by Shanghai Electric, Shanghai International Port Group, and CMA CGM Group. Representatives from relevant government departments, industry associations, scientific research institutions, financial institutions, and industry chain cooperation partners witnessed the bunkering activity.

According to the plan, the second phase of Shanghai Electric's Jilin Taonan green hydrogen coupled with biomass integrated green methanol-oil project will officially start construction on August 20 and is expected to be fully completed and put into operation in 2028. After commissioning, the project will have an annual capacity of 200 kt of green methanol and 10 kt of sustainable aviation fuel, providing more fuel security for the green and low-carbon transition of the shipping and aviation sectors.

text:
Mass balancing could be key to unlocking biomethane as a scalable marine fuel option for shipping by 2030, according to a new analysis by the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping (MMMCZCS).

The report published on Tuesday estimates global biomethane supply could reach around 21 billion cubic metres (bcm) by 2030 in a base case, rising to 52 bcm in a policy-driven scenario.

The study estimates the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework could create unconstrained demand equivalent to around 30 bcm of biomethane in 2030 if the fuel met the entire demand for low-emissions energy.

This means biomethane could theoretically cover around 70% of shipping’s 2030 demand for low-emissions energy in the base case.

However, the report stresses that actual uptake would be lower, with the methane-capable fleet, bunkering infrastructure and competition from other sectors limiting demand.

Mass balancing is identified as a critical enabler. It would allow biomethane to be injected into existing natural gas networks, with its environmental attributes tracked through a certified chain of custody and allocated to maritime fuel consumption.

Without such a framework, shipping would largely depend on physically segregated biomethane supply chains, which the report says would be difficult and costly to scale before 2030.

“However, if the IMO allows globally harmonized mass balancing, biomethane could be injected into the existing natural gas grid, with its sustainability attributes tracked through a certified chain of custody and allocated to maritime fuel consumption,” it said.

The analysis concludes that biomethane could provide significant early compliance abatement while other fuels, including e-ammonia and e-methanol, scale up.

title: Phased fuel transitions for decarbonizing the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor - Nature

text:
International maritime shipping is a fundamental sector of global trade, facilitating approximately 90% of the world’s merchandise movement1. Yet, it remains a substantial emitter of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, contributing roughly 3% of the global emissions2. Despite mounting regulatory pressures, the sector’s decarbonization progress remains limited, with over 99% of its energy still derived from fossil fuels3, highlighting a stark disconnect between ambitious net-zero targets and the current pace of transition. In response, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has progressively strengthened its emissions reduction targets. Its 2018 Initial GHG Strategy aimed to halve annual emissions by 20504, which was updated in 2023 through a Revised Strategy committing to achieve net-zero GHG emissions ‘by or around 2050’. The revised strategy also sets stricter interim targets: a 40% reduction by 2030 and 70–80% by 2040 (relative to a 2008 baseline)5. To realize these ambitions, the IMO has proposed a Net-Zero Framework prioritizing the expansion of biofuels and other alternative fuels within the maritime energy portfolio6. Although the formal adoption of this framework has been delayed7, global momentum towards achieving net-zero emissions continues. This is exemplified by regional initiatives such as the European Union (EU)’s FuelEU Maritime regulation, set to launch in 20258, which aims to accelerate the transition and serve as a testing ground for decarbonization pathways.

Navigating this complex, multipolicy landscape to identify viable transition pathways under deep uncertainty is therefore a critical challenge. In this context, Green Shipping Corridors, defined as specific maritime routes where stakeholders collaborate to adopt zero-emission fuels ahead of broader industry timelines, have emerged as a strategic focal point9. Focusing on a central corridor, such as the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor, can therefore reduce investment risks and develop scalable industry-wide decarbonization solutions.

In practice, deep decarbonization faces multiple hurdles. Existing ship technologies, such as onboard emission capture systems, can deliver only moderate emission reductions10. Port infrastructure upgrades also require extended lead times and are often misaligned with regulatory timeframes11. In addition, electric ships are not yet viable for long-distance routes12. Consequently, the large-scale deployment of low-carbon alternative fuels, such as hydrogen, ammonia, methanol and biofuels13, has increasingly been recognized as the most feasible pathway to meet the targets of the FuelEU Maritime regulation and the IMO Net-Zero Framework.

However, reliably evaluating this critical fuel transition under real-world conditions is complex. Shipping regulations and technologies are shifting, as illustrated by the delay in approving the IMO Net-Zero Framework, creating persistent uncertainty. Current analytical tools, however, are not equipped to fully capture this complexity. Traditional assessment frameworks, primarily based on static life cycle assessment (LCA)14,15 or limited dynamic projections16, offer only snapshot comparisons that fail to account for the critical feedback loops through which technical learning curves, fuel adoption and infrastructure deployment interact and co-evolve, the factors that ultimately determine the long-term feasibility of transition pathways. Furthermore, most existing pathway analyses treat regulations as static, external factors rather than as endogenous variables that interact dynamically with technological and economic factors17,18.

To address this gap, we developed a dynamic LCA framework that integrates system dynamics (SD), moving beyond static snapshots to capture the evolving, multidimensional performance of alternative marine fuels through 2050. It assesses four dimensions: climate impacts, environmental sustainability, energy efficiency and economic feasibility (termed Climate-3E). The framework is applied to a critical case study: the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor, selected for its high trade volume and potential exposure to dual regulatory pressures from the IMO Net-Zero Framework and the FuelEU Maritime regulation. The analysis encompasses 13 alternative fuels, benchmarked against heavy fuel oil (HFO) and marine diesel oil (MDO), including biodiesel, denoted as soybean-based fatty acid methyl ester (FAME); methanol variants: coal-based (Coal-MeOH), natural gas-based (NG-MeOH), electro-MeOH (e-MeOH) and bio-derived (bio-MeOH); liquefied natural gas variants: conventional (Conv-LNG), electro-LNG (e-LNG) and bio-derived (bio-LNG); liquid hydrogen variants: conventional (Conv-LH2), electro-LH2 (e-LH2) and bio-derived (bio-LH2); liquid ammonia variants: conventional (Conv-LNH3) and electro-LNH3 (e-LNH3).

This study addresses a central question for the maritime low-carbon transition: which fuel transition pathways can most effectively decarbonize global shipping under the evolving IMO Net-Zero Framework and the FuelEU Maritime regulation? The proposed dynamic modelling framework reveals how policy timing and regulatory stringency may shape future mitigation outcomes, clarifying the conditions under which alternative fuels gain or lose competitiveness. While the modelling framework cannot encompass all factors influencing decision-making, it provides forward-looking, scenario-based projections of fuel competitiveness and transition trajectories, thereby empowering shipowners, policymakers and investors to make informed decisions. By illuminating the dynamic interplay of policy, technology and fuel competitiveness, this study supports confident, timely commitments to the most robust and scalable pathways for a climate-resilient maritime future.

Current status and prospects of alternative marine fuels

A comprehensive LCA is conducted to evaluate the decarbonization potential of marine fuels by quantifying their Climate-3E performance (climate impacts, environmental sustainability, energy efficiency and economic feasibility) relative to baseline HFO and MDO. Across 1,300 scenarios (Supplementary Fig. 3) reflecting diverse production pathways and operational conditions, the assessment reveals a spectrum of performance for alternative fuels, as detailed in Fig. 1.

Figure 1a shows that hydrogen-based marine fuels, particularly electro- and bio-LH2, achieve near-zero life cycle GHG emissions in most scenarios. Conv-LH2 also delivers substantial GHG emission reduction compared with HFO and MDO. However, the low energy density of hydrogen fuels limits their practical use, often requiring 30–70% blending with diesel on long voyages, diminishing overall climate benefits19,20. Bio-LNG emerges as a viable transitional fuel, offering substantial emission reductions due to biogenic carbon uptake21. By contrast, Conv-LNG exhibits higher life cycle emissions than HFO and MDO due to methane leakage and the energy-intensive liquefaction process22. E-LNG performs between bio-LNG and HFO under current energy structures. All LNG-based pathways retain lower long-term emissions, underscoring their continued relevance for the low-carbon transition.

Conversely, methanol- and ammonia-based fuels, including their electrofuel (e-fuel) variants, generally exhibit higher life cycle emissions than HFO and MDO, because their low energy density increases fuel consumption per distance travelled, and fossil-derived variants (Coal-MeOH, NG-MeOH and Conv-LNH3) rely on carbon-intensive synthesis23. While bio-MeOH offers meaningful emission reduction, the climate performance of e-MeOH and e-LNH3 remains strongly constrained by the carbon intensity of the electricity mix. Under current fossil-dominated grids, their carbon footprints may exceed those of HFO and MDO.

Figure 1b–d compares the carbon intensity indicator (CII) (a regulatory metric established by the IMO to quantify operational carbon efficiency), energy efficiency and economic viability24,25. HFO and MDO exhibit high CII values due to their high tank-to-wake emissions resulting from the combustion of carbon-intensive hydrocarbons26,27. Biofuels, by contrast, demonstrate balanced advantages. For example, bio-MeOH, bio-LNG and bio-LH2 may achieve emission reductions of 41.5%, 47.4% and 31.1%, respectively, compared with HFO and offer more favourable energy and economic profiles than most e-fuel alternatives. However, scalability and slightly higher costs remain barriers, and e-fuels provide deep emission reductions when powered by renewable electricity28, but their production remains highly energy-intensive29. The electrolysis process for hydrogen production, a foundational stage for all these e-fuels, entails substantial energy conversion losses30, and both carbon capture and electrolysis technologies exhibit high costs28,31,32. As a result, their current market competitiveness remains low, with only 11.1–35.6% of HFO.

Technological advancements are expected to shift this landscape. Rapid investment in e-fuels and direct air capture of atmospheric CO2 is expanding production potential33,34. By 2050, the Climate-3E performance of e-LNG, bio-MeOH, e-LNH3 and e-MeOH is projected to surpass that of HFO and MDO. Meanwhile, the results also reveal policy-dependent divergence. While the Climate-3E performance under both policies is closely aligned, the FuelEU Maritime regulation provides more substantial economic incentives for fuel transition compared with the IMO Net-Zero Framework (Supplementary Figs. 16–18).

Sensitivity analysis shows that e-fuels (e-MeOH and e-LNG) exhibit greater stability against carbon price fluctuations (±20%) than fossil-derived and biomass-derived fuels, which show greater volatility in emissions and costs (Supplementary Fig. 10). Life cycle impact assessment results indicate that biofuels offer cobenefits such as lower acidification and eutrophication potentials. At the same time, certain e-fuels and ammonia pathways entail higher human and ecotoxicity burdens under the current energy system (Supplementary Fig. 11). A breakdown of life cycle costs confirms that fuel costs dominate, with e-MeOH the most expensive and Conv-LNG among the most cost-competitive alternatives when ship modifications and maintenance are considered (Supplementary Fig. 12). These findings underscore that, while e-fuels promise long-term decarbonization and price resilience, biofuels present a balanced near-term profile with favourable environmental cobenefits, albeit with scalability constraints.

How the electricity mix shapes e-fuel performance

The performance of e-fuels is powerfully shaped by the carbon intensity of the electricity used in their production. To evaluate this influence in a strategic decarbonization context, this study focuses on the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor, which has high trade volumes and is likely to face dual regulatory pressures from the IMO Net-Zero Framework and the EU’s FuelEU Maritime regulation. Figure 2 summarizes the installed renewable power generation capacity along this corridor35, highlighting regional disparities that underlie fuel competitiveness.

East Asia has the highest renewable power capacity (649 GW), while Western Europe leads in the share of renewables within its electricity mix. To assess the impact, fuel performance is compared under the current electricity mix and renewable power scenario using the Climate-3E framework. Results for the EU are shown in Fig. 3 (results for other regions along the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor shown are in Supplementary Fig. 15).

From a climate perspective (Fig. 3a), renewable electricity is pivotal for e-fuels to achieve deep-life cycle GHG cuts. Conventional and biomass-derived fuels, such as Coal-MeOH, NG-MeOH, Conv-LNG and bio-variants, exhibit limited sensitivity to the electricity mix, whereas e-fuels show pronounced variation. Under the renewable electricity scenario, e-LNG and e-LNH3 achieve low emissions, while e-MeOH remains carbon-intensive due to process-related N2O and CH4 emissions during synthesis36.

Environmental performance (Fig. 3b) further illustrates the influence37. The carbon intensity of e-fuels declines substantially as renewable electricity penetration increases. Biofuels remain stable in carbon intensity because they rely little on electricity. Under the renewable scenario, Conv-LNH3 achieves a carbon intensity of 0.002 kg of CO2 per tonne·nautical mile, below the regulatory benchmark, and both e-MeOH and e-LNG can attain negative carbon intensity.

Energy performance (Fig. 3c) shows that renewable power has a limited impact on conventional and biomass-derived fuels, whose life cycle energy consumption depends on the feedstock and process technology. By contrast, renewable power substantially reduces the energy intensity of e-fuel production33. For example, the life cycle energy consumption of renewable-powered e-MeOH, e-LNG and e-LNH3 is reduced by 57.2%, 56.8% and 41.5%, respectively. This improvement stems from the higher efficiency of renewable electricity systems relative to fossil-derived thermal generation. Economic outcomes (Fig. 3d) are less responsive to changes in the electricity mix. However, the declining cost of renewable energy enhances the long-term competitiveness of e-fuels38,39. Continued advances in renewable technologies and the scaling of e-fuel production are expected to strengthen their economic viability further.

Annual costs and emissions under dual regulatory scenarios

The transition to low-carbon marine fuels is a long-term, dynamic, path-dependent process. An analysis is therefore essential to capture total emissions over the transition period, avoiding misinterpretation from short-term fluctuations. Guided by this perspective, transition outcomes across key regions along the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor—from Japan, through China (East Asia), Malaysia (Southeast Asia), the United Arab Emirates (Middle East), Egypt (Africa), to Europe—are compared under different policy scenarios, as simulated in Fig. 4.

Figure 4 compares annual carbon emissions under three scenarios: Business as Usual (BAU), the Most Economical (ME) and the Maximum Carbon Reduction (MCR) for the IMO Net-Zero Framework-only, the FuelEU Maritime-only and two policies combined. The IMO Net-Zero Framework has considerable potential to align economically viable and low-emission pathways across regions. By contrast, the FuelEU Maritime could lead to greater divergence between these objectives. This contrast reflects fundamental differences in policy design. The IMO Net-Zero Framework combines stringent annual carbon-intensity reductions with a two-tier carbon-emission penalty system (US$100 per tonne CO2 equivalent (CO2e) for tier 1 and US$380 per tonne CO2e for tier 2)40. By contrast, the EU applies more gradual carbon-intensity targets, but imposes a higher carbon-emission penalty of US$730 per tonne CO2e41, nearly twice the IMO tier 2 rate. Because Conv-LNG can meet EU compliance standards for an extended period and provides high economic efficiency, shipowners are incentivized to continue using Conv-LNG as an alternative fuel, suppressing the growth of e-fuels. Conversely, the IMO’s stricter trajectory discourages long-term reliance on transitional fossil fuel options, accelerating the competitiveness and uptake of e-fuels and biofuels.

Regional outcomes reflect these regulatory dynamics. Under the IMO Net-Zero Framework, Japan’s ME and MCR pathways yield similar annual carbon emissions, indicating strong convergence between economic and environmental objectives. Compared with the IMO Net-Zero Framework-only scenario, the two policies combined scenario yields only a small difference in annual carbon emissions. This is because, under the combined regime, the overall carbon emission trajectory converges towards the more stringent IMO targets, restricting prolonged use of transitional fuels and thus preventing a substantial divergence between the ME and MCR pathways. However, under the FuelEU Maritime-only scenario, a clear gap exists between economic and environmental objectives within China, which widens in regions with electricity systems dominated by renewable energy. Conversely, it can narrow further in the carbon-intensive regions. Because Conv-LNG only ensures near-term compliance at low cost, it pulls carbon-intensive regions towards similar ME and MCR emissions trajectories, thereby accelerating the transition to cleaner fuels. These findings demonstrate that the FuelEU Maritime’s lenient carbon-intensity targets may inadvertently prolong the use of conventional fuels, even imposing higher penalties, particularly in regions with high renewable penetration. By contrast, the IMO Net-Zero Framework’s annually tightened emission-mitigation targets can promote both emission reductions and economic feasibility across regions without imposing disproportionately higher costs, thereby enabling more consistent global progress towards maritime decarbonization.

Technological pathways for marine fuel transitions

The adoption of alternative marine fuels involves distinct technological strategies to achieve decarbonization (Supplementary Fig. 8). Current methods include drop-in fuel blending, retrofitting conventional engines and deploying new dual-fuel engines capable of operating on MeOH, LH2 or LNH3 (refs. 42,43). Figure 5 presents projected fuel strategies from 2024 to 2050, along with their associated carbon intensity and relative costs, under two regulatory scenarios: the FuelEU Maritime-only scenario and the two policies combined scenario, revealing distinct technological trajectories. Drop-in biodiesel blending with MDO offers meaningful near-term emission reductions, lowering carbon intensity to 0.047 kg of CO2e per megajoule. However, this pathway remains economically constrained and fails to comply with the IMO targets beyond 2035, serving only as a short-term transitional measure.

Newbuild dual-fuel engines exhibit more complex and policy-dependent outcomes. While e-MeOH delivers low life cycle carbon emissions, its economic performance varies considerably across policies. It remains relatively affordable under the FuelEU Maritime-only scenario, but becomes more expensive under the two policies combined scenario. Both e-LNG and bio-LNG show strong decarbonization potential, whereas Conv-LH2 and Conv-LNH3 remain cost-effective but carbon-intensive. Their electro-counterparts face substantial technical hurdles: hydrogen still requires substantial diesel blending, and ammonia relies on partial diesel use; both incur high compliance costs, especially under the IMO Net-Zero Framework-only scenario (Supplementary Fig. 19). This scenario supports e-LNG and bio-LNG, while the FuelEU Maritime-only scenario supports e-MeOH and e-LNG. Under the combined policy scenario, however, high carbon compliance costs raise the cost of conventional fuels such as HFO, thereby enhancing the economic viability of other low-carbon alternatives, notably e-LH2 and e-LNH3. These comparisons illustrate that the selection of a technological pathway is not determined solely by inherent fuel qualities but is influenced by the policy framework.

Achieving deep decarbonization in the shipping industry requires diverse, multistage transition pathways that account for the distinct production routes and performance profiles of alternative marine fuels. From a climate perspective, biodiesel, hydrogen and bio-LNG offer substantial potential to reduce life cycle GHG emissions. By contrast, fossil-derived alternatives provide limited climate benefits due to their energy-intensive production processes. Economically, Conv-LNG already delivers notable cost savings over HFO and MDO, while other biofuels such as bio-MeOH and bio-LNG remain moderately more expensive, and e-fuels still carry a substantial price premium. Overall, biofuels represent the most balanced near-term options, offering a viable combination of economic competitiveness and tangible emission reductions.

A critical perspective emerges when considering the inherent uncertainties in these comparisons. The probability distributions of the Climate-3E metrics from the Monte Carlo analysis (Supplementary Fig. 9) quantify this uncertainty, revealing a spectrum of possible outcomes. This underscores that the real-world viability of any pathway cannot be judged solely by its average performance. For instance, the wide distribution of the CII highlights a tangible compliance risk for several fuels under variable operating conditions. This performance uncertainty translates directly into economic risks. The sensitivity of fossil-derived and biomass-derived pathways to carbon price fluctuations (Supplementary Fig. 10) exposes early adopters to substantial financial and regulatory volatility. Conversely, the price resilience of e-fuels offers a long-term hedge. Therefore, the fuel transition is not merely a cost–emission trade-off but a strategic choice between accepting short-term volatility or investing in long-term predictability. This uncertainty-aware perspective calls for policies that not only penalize emissions but also actively derisk investments in stable, deep-decarbonization technologies.

Regional variation in electricity mixes further shapes the suitability of fuels along green shipping corridors. In regions with a high share of renewable electricity, e-fuels achieve notable reductions in GHG emissions and carbon intensity, demonstrating strong long-term decarbonization potential. Conversely, where fossil fuels dominate the electricity mix, the carbon intensity of e-fuels remains high, severely limiting their environmental value. The prospects of biofuels, meanwhile, depend on the availability of biomass feedstock (Supplementary Information section IV). Given the decisive role of clean electricity in determining life cycle emissions, addressing regional differences in power generation is essential to designing effective transition pathways. Efforts should therefore focus on deploying location-appropriate fuels, expanding renewable capacity in fossil-dependent regions and preparing the infrastructure necessary for future large-scale e-fuel adoption.

Maritime decarbonization is further shaped by regulatory architecture. The FuelEU Maritime regulation advances emissions reductions through a penalty system and moderate carbon-intensity targets, enabling meaningful reductions in specific contexts. However, its effectiveness varies by region. In areas with cleaner power grids, Conv-LNG is likely to retain a long-term compliance advantage due to its lower costs, potentially slowing the adoption of higher-cost, lower-emission alternatives. Conversely, in regions with carbon-intensive grids, transition fuels cannot meet long-term compliance requirements, prompting a shift to alternative fuels to avoid steep penalties, thereby accelerating the transition to low-carbon fuels and amplifying shipping decarbonization outcomes.

In comparison, the IMO Net-Zero Framework uses a two-tier carbon-pricing mechanism coupled with strict, annually tightening carbon-intensity targets. This design steadily narrows the gap between the most economical pathways and those with the strongest emission reductions, effectively balancing environmental ambition with economic feasibility. Consequently, the IMO Net-Zero Framework promotes greater convergence in decarbonization pathways across regions with heterogeneous electricity mixes, demonstrating broader applicability. It provides a more globally balanced approach, integrating environmental rigour with economic practicality and supporting scalable transition strategies. When the FuelEU Maritime regulation is already in place, layering the IMO Net-Zero Framework on top can further reduce the cost differential between alternative and conventional marine fuels. As a comprehensive global benchmark, the IMO Net-Zero Framework is better positioned to deliver consistent, equitable and scalable progress towards decarbonizing international shipping.

The integrated LCA–SD framework

To dynamically evaluate the multidimensional performance and transition pathways of alternative marine fuels, we developed an integrated framework combining LCA and SD (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). Among various scenario-based projection approaches, SD modelling is particularly well suited due to its ability to transparently represent the interactions among system elements, making results more interpretable and easier to validate. In addition, SD can simulate dynamic behaviour and account for feedback effects over time44. This method has been widely applied in the energy sector to project technology diffusion and policy impacts. Its main advantage lies in its capacity to integrate multiple subsystems, aligning with the multistage, interactive nature of LCA. The SD model was constructed and simulated in Vensim PLE (version 10.4.0), in which the model’s causal structure, including key feedback loops related to policy compliance, technology costs, fuel adoption decisions and infrastructure investment, was formally represented as a stock-and-flow diagram (Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). A comprehensive review of prior static and dynamic LCA studies, along with a systematic comparison of alternative methodologies, is provided in Supplementary Tables 1–3.

The assessment follows an eight-step process organized into two interlinked phases. The first phase involves a static LCA to establish a robust, multidimensional baseline of fuel performance. We began by defining the scope of the analysis, focusing on the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor, selecting 13 alternative marine fuels. Key operational parameters, including representative containership sizes, were specified. The functional unit was defined as ‘per tonne·nautical mile’ of cargo transported. A ‘well-to-wake’ system boundary was applied to each fuel pathway, covering the complete life cycle from feedstock extraction and fuel production through storage, transportation and final combustion in the ship’s engine. A detailed life cycle inventory was then developed by integrating data on energy and material flows from fuel production processes and operational profiles. To account for inherent data variability, key inventory parameters were assigned probability distributions. The static performance of all fuel pathways for a reference year was then quantified by calculating the four assessment dimensions, climate impacts, environmental sustainability, energy efficiency and economic feasibility (Climate-3E), based on the life cycle inventory. Monte Carlo simulations45,46 and sensitivity analysis were conducted to characterize uncertainty, yielding probability distributions for each indicator. In addition, a life cycle impact assessment47,48 was conducted across multiple environmental indicators to evaluate broader environmental trade-offs. Detailed inventory data sources, scenario specifications and parameter values are provided in Supplementary Information section II.

The second phase involves dynamic SD modelling, which projects how the baseline evolves in response to the interplay of policy, market and technological change. The initial input parameters for the SD model were derived from statistically representative values of the Climate-3E indicators from the static LCA. We then embedded the core mechanisms of the IMO Net-Zero Framework and the EU’s FuelEU Maritime regulation by translating key LCA outputs into dynamic variables that influence compliance costs and decision-making over time. The conceptual feedback structure was translated into a set of mathematical equations that explicitly model policy mechanisms, technology learning curves, biofuel supply constraint driven by the price elasticity, and feedback loops linking fuel economics to adoption decisions. This enabled us to simulate system behaviour quantitatively from 2024 to 2050. The validity of the SD model’s behavioural dynamics was tested by comparing its simulated output for a historical period against observed industry trends (Supplementary Fig. 7). Once validated, the model was used to project future fuel pathways, annual carbon emissions and the evolution of Climate-3E performance through 2050 under various scenarios. Detailed SD model equations, variable definitions and data sources are provided in Supplementary Information section III.

Policy scenario

This study examines three distinct regulatory scenarios to understand their individual and combined effects on the fuel transition (Supplementary Fig. 4). The first scenario models the IMO Net-Zero Framework, incorporating its ambitious targets and economic mechanisms, including increasingly strict annual limits on GHG intensity, a two-tier penalty system and its flexibility provisions. The second scenario models the EU’s FuelEU Maritime regulation, which mandates a gradual reduction in the average carbon intensity of energy used by ships calling at EU ports. This includes imposing a penalty of US$730 per tonne of CO2e for non-compliance and accounting for flexibility regulations, such as banking, pooling and the 50% emissions requirement for voyages involving only one EU port. The third scenario combines both frameworks, where vessels must comply with both sets of rules. In this case, more stringent requirements apply to each compliance element, and the total compliance cost is the sum of expenses incurred under each policy. This combined scenario tests the interaction and potential synergy or conflict between the global, market-based IMO policy and the regional, prescriptive EU regulation.

Assumptions and limitations

The integrated LCA–SD framework is based on several assumptions and has certain limitations. Due to the complexity of allocating shipping emissions on a global scale, this study models a round-trip voyage along the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor, starting and ending at the same port. It assumes a consistent fuel blend throughout the journey, a simplification that allows clear comparison of fuels across electricity mixes and policies. For biofuels, the supply elasticity of bio-LNG is set higher than that of other biofuels, reflecting the assumption that its primary feedstocks, organic waste and residues, are widely available and can be scaled readily with demand (Supplementary Figs. 13 and 14). As the IMO Net-Zero Framework does not specify targets beyond 2040, the post-2040 ‘Base Target’ and ‘Direct Compliance Target’ values are adopted from an external source49. The framework’s potential reward mechanism for zero-carbon fuels is not modelled, as its monetary value and operational details remain undefined, and very few fuels would qualify. The EU Emissions Trading System is not explicitly incorporated; instead, the FuelEU Maritime penalty price is used to represent the overall economic incentive from the broader EU policy mix. The model simplifies real-world operations by fixing a round-trip pattern, which may not capture all operational variability. Projections depend on technology learning curves and cost reductions, which are subject to future uncertainty, and regional electricity mixes may evolve differently over time. Furthermore, the model does not account for ship-operator behavioural responses, future regulatory changes or macroeconomic shocks, all of which are important areas for further research.

text:
International shipping still relies on fossil fuels for more than 99% of its energy. However, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) Net-Zero Framework and the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime regulation are pushing the sector towards cleaner fuels. Despite this, we still lack clear evidence on which alternative marine fuels work best under changing regulations and across climate and cost factors. Without such evidence, shipowners and policymakers cannot judge which fuel pathways are most practical or when cleaner fuels may become affordable. They also cannot see clearly how local electricity systems shape the performance of different fuels. This evidence gap is particularly urgent because new ships and fuel infrastructure take years to plan and build. The policy challenge is to provide a forward-looking analysis to turn these regulatory goals into practical, cost-effective fuel transition strategies.

We find that soybean-based biodiesel is a viable near-term solution, while bio-LNG can cut emissions by up to 47.4% compared with heavy fuel oil. Electrofuels become more cost-competitive after 2040 as production costs and electricity systems become cleaner. Policy design matters greatly: the IMO Net-Zero Framework (which tightens targets and introduces a two-tier penalty system) more consistently pushes the sector towards lower-emission fuels. By contrast, the FuelEU Maritime regulation is particularly effective in carbon-intensive regions, accelerating the phase-out of fossil fuels. In regions with clean grids, policy adjustments are needed to prevent transitional fuels from gaining compliance advantages that could delay the uptake of zero-emissions fuels. Regional electricity supply is critical to the performance of electricity-based fuels, which work best where renewable power is already abundant (Fig. 1). This analysis does not account for operator behaviour or market shifts, so policy frameworks should remain adaptable to local conditions.

We compared 13 alternative marine fuels for the Asia–Europe Green Shipping Corridor from 2024 to 2050 using a framework that links the life cycle impacts of each fuel to changes in technology, policy and costs over time. The framework assesses four key dimensions: climate impacts, environmental sustainability, energy efficiency and economic feasibility. It examines how the IMO Net-Zero Framework and the FuelEU Maritime regulation affect fuel choices, both individually and together. It also allows policymakers to test how changes in carbon intensity targets, penalty structures or electricity supply could affect which fuels are most attractive over time. By providing forward-looking projections based on real-world corridor conditions, the framework offers a practical basis for tailoring maritime decarbonization strategies to different regional contexts.

text:
Safety requirements for hydrogen-, methanol- and ethanol-fuelled ships had been revised, Japanese classification society ClassNK said on Tuesday.

The changes are contained in Edition 3.1 of its Guidelines for Ships Using Alternative Fuels.

ClassNK is a third-party certification body that develops technical standards and provides classification and certification services for ships.

The revised section covering hydrogen-fuelled vessels incorporated the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Interim Guidelines for the Safety of Ships Using Hydrogen as Fuel, the society said.

It also introduces estimated hydrogen-leak frequencies that may be used in safety assessments required under the IMO guidelines for the approval of alternative-fuelled vessels by administrations.

A Bayesian statistical method had been used to derive the estimates by combining newly observed data with existing information, ClassNK said.

The hydrogen-leak frequency estimates have been included in an appendix to the revised guidelines.

They were intended to enable ship designs and the associated safety assessments to be conducted on a more consistent basis, said the society.

The IMO’s interim guidelines were finalised during the 11th session of its Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers in September 2025 and issued this year.

ClassNK participated in their development as a member of the Japanese delegation to the subcommittee, the society said.

The revised edition also introduces structural-strength requirements for fuel tanks used on methanol- and ethanol-fuelled vessels.

Those requirements were not specifically stipulated in the IMO’s 2020 guidelines for the safety of ships using methanol and ethanol as fuel, said ClassNK.

They were developed using the society’s experience in reviewing the design of methanol- and ethanol-fuelled ships and are intended to standardise fuel-tank structural assessments.

ClassNK’s alternative-fuel guidelines also set out requirements for equipment, controls and safety devices on vessels using liquefied petroleum gas and ammonia.

text:
Shanghai Port has completed the world’s largest single green methanol bunkering operation, supplying 8,016 tonnes of domestically produced green methanol to a dual-fuel container ship owned by French shipping and logistics company CMA CGM.

The fuel was delivered by the bunkering vessel Haigang Zhiyuan to the CMA CGM Osium at Yangshan Port in Shanghai over the weekend, Shanghai Customs said on Monday.

The operation set a global record for the largest amount of green methanol supplied in a single bunkering operation.

Shanghai Electric Group President Zhu Zhaokai said the operation also marked the development of an integrated green methanol supply chain in China. It covers large-scale production, onshore and offshore storage, transportation, port bunkering and the use of the fuel on ships.

Zhu said the model could provide a solution that can be expanded and repeated for the green and low-carbon transformation of international shipping.

Shanghai has supplied a total of 36,000 tonnes of green methanol to vessels since China’s first green methanol bunkering operation in April 2024, according to Shanghai Customs. The port now ranks first among major global ports in cumulative green methanol bunkering, it said.

To support growing demand, Shanghai Customs has introduced 10 measures to make operations easier for international-voyage vessels. It has also created a digital system to monitor the green-fuel bunkering process from start to finish.

Officials said the system helps reduce vessel turnaround times and lower logistics costs.

Green methanol is produced using biomass resources and renewable energy instead of fossil fuels. It is considered one of the alternative fuels that can help reduce carbon emissions in shipping, chemicals and other industries.

The use of green methanol is expected to grow as the global shipping industry moves towards cleaner energy sources.

China’s newly issued 15th Five-Year Plan for Building a Beautiful China calls for traditional industries to be upgraded with greener technologies while supporting the growth of green sectors.

China’s green and low-carbon industries have a market worth about 11 trillion yuan ($1.62 trillion) and include more than 2 million enterprises, according to the source material.
