text:
A brutal jurisdictional conflict between the federal government and California state regulators threatens to severely disrupt international supply chains and spike consumer prices. At the epicenter of this conflict lies California's Commercial Harbor Craft regulation, an aggressive environmental mandate designed to eliminate diesel particulate emissions from marine vessels operating within state waters.

The Trump administration, prioritizing sweeping deregulation and the reduction of logistics costs, has launched a coordinated assault against California's unique authority to dictate environmental standards. The outcome of this battle will determine whether the maritime industry faces massive compliance costs or secures a permanent reprieve from state-level climate mandates.

The Commercial Harbor Craft Mandate

The regulation requires operators of tugboats, ferries, and commercial harbor craft to install highly complex, heavily expensive diesel particulate filters on their marine engines. Industry experts and maritime engineers maintain that the technology remains largely unproven for the harsh realities of marine operations.

The Technological Barrier: Diesel particulate filters require extremely high, consistent operating temperatures to incinerate captured pollution. The variable, start-and-stop engine loads typical of towing vessels prevent the filters from functioning safely, creating severe fire hazards.

The Financial Burden: Retrofitting a single harbor vessel with experimental filtration systems can cost millions of dollars. The limited market size for marine specific filters prevents economies of scale, keeping research and development costs prohibitively high.

The Federal Intervention: The federal Environmental Protection Agency has aggressively intervened, referring California's regulatory waiver to Congress for review under the Congressional Review Act, actively attempting to strip the state of its statutory authority.

If California successfully enforces the mandate, port operators warn that logistics companies will simply pass the exorbitant retrofit costs down the supply chain. This would directly inflate the price of imported consumer goods, electronics, and agricultural exports flowing through the critical ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach.

The Countervailing Tariff Threat

The environmental cost dispute is unfolding against the backdrop of the administration's aggressive trade posture. President Trump has repeatedly proposed expansive global tariffs and instituted a specialized infrastructure fee targeting all foreign-built ships docking at domestic ports.

The proposed Maritime Action Plan includes infrastructure fees ranging from one cent to twenty-five cents per kilogram of imported cargo. At the higher end of that spectrum, maritime analysts project the fees could extract USD 1.5 trillion (KES 195 trillion) from global shipping over the next decade. Industry leaders argue that compounding punitive federal tariffs with radical state-level environmental mandates will paralyze the maritime sector, driving operators into bankruptcy and crippling the national economy.

Supply Chain Vulnerabilities in Emerging Markets

The regulatory battles unfolding in California serve as a critical warning indicator for global logistics, particularly across the African continent. The ports of Mombasa in Kenya and Dar es Salaam in Tanzania rely overwhelmingly on older, diesel-powered fleets to manage bulk cargo and container transshipments. These vital economic arteries operate on razor-thin margins.

If the International Maritime Organization adopts California-style emission standards as global best practices, East African port authorities will face a devastating crisis. The capital required to retrofit the aging tugboat and harbor craft fleets operating in the Indian Ocean simply does not exist within current maritime budgets. Forcing compliance would necessitate catastrophic increases in port handling fees, instantly elevating the cost of vital imports, including wheat, fertilizer, and refined petroleum.

The federal challenge to California's authority represents a broader philosophical war over the cost of the green transition. As the EPA moves to dismantle the regulatory framework, the maritime industry remains trapped in regulatory purgatory, unable to execute long-term capital investments while the courts decide the fate of America's coastal economy.

text:
Notice to all Owners, Masters, Officers, Ratings and those concerned with maritime training.

This notice replaces MIN 729 (M+F).

1. Purpose of this amendment

This notice replaces MIN 729 and provides updated UK MCA policy regarding the implementation of IMO Resolution MSC.560(108) in relation to Personal Safety and Social Responsibilities (PSSR).

To support implementation, the MCA is introducing a free, online and accessible training module to assist seafarers and companies in meeting the updated competence requirements in a consistent, straightforward and supportive manner.

2. Background

IMO Resolution MSC.560(108), adopted on 23 May 2024, introduced amendments to STCW Code Table A‑VI/1‑4, including new mandatory competence relating to:

“Contribute to the prevention of and response to violence and harassment, including sexual harassment, bullying and sexual assault.”

These amendments entered into force on 1 January 2026.

The amendments require seafarers to demonstrate knowledge of:

prevention of violence and harassment

identification and reporting of such behaviours

understanding impacts on safety, health and wellbeing

appropriate response and support, including trauma‑informed principles

3. Revised MCA policy: applicability to all seafarers

As previously set out in MIN 729 (M+F), further clarification was being sought at the IMO regarding the requirement for all seafarers to complete training covering the additional competence introduced by MSC.560(108).

Following the outcome of the IMO working group and the findings of the HTW Sub-Committee session (February 2026), the MCA position has now been revised

The MCA now requires, for the purposes of demonstrating compliance with STCW Table A‑VI/1‑4, that:

all seafarers, who are required to hold a PSSR Certificate must complete additional training covering the new competence introduced by MSC.560(108). The MCA has developed a free e-learning module to meet this requirement set out in section 4 and 8

However:

all MCA-approved PSSR courses completed on or after 1 January 2026 include this additional learning outcome

therefore, candidates holding an MCA-approved PSSR certificate dated on or after 1 January 2026 are not required to complete the supplementary e-learning module

This revision reflects IMO decisions and ensures:

consistent compliance with updated STCW requirements, and

the promotion of safe and respectful working environments across the maritime sector

4. Mandatory training requirement

4.1 Requirement

All seafarers, regardless of rank, who are employed or engaged in any capacity on board a ship, as part of the ship’s complement, with designated safety or pollution prevention duties in the operation of the vessel, are required to undertake this training.

All of the following must complete the additional training:

holders of UK PSSR certificate (A-VI/1-4) dated before 1 January 2026

holders of UK Certificates of Competency (CoC)

holders of UK Certificates of Proficiency (CoP)

all UK-certified officers and ratings

4.2 Approved delivery method

The MCA has arranged for this requirement to be met through the:

This online module:

is aligned with STCW requirements under Table A‑VI/1‑4

covers prevention, identification, response and reporting

is available free of charge to all UK seafarers and UK-MCA certified seafarers

is available to take 24 hours a day

can also be taken on a mobile phone

should take around 1 hour to complete

has no final assessment

5. Deadline for completion

Failure to complete the training by this date may affect:

certificate revalidation

demonstration of compliance during inspections

eligibility to work on vessels at sea

6. Evidence of completion

Upon successful completion of the module:

seafarers will receive a OneOcean Verification of Training document

this verification shall be accepted by the MCA as valid evidence of having completed the required training

6.1 Use of verification

The Verification of Training may be presented as evidence for:

new or revalidation of UK CoC or CoP

Port State Control or Flag State inspection, if asked

requests by an authorised officer

The accepted format is digital only.

No additional certificate will be required by the MCA.

7. Responsibilities of companies and seafarers

7.1 Companies

Companies should:

ensure all UK-certified personnel complete the module within the required timeframe

maintain records of training completion

promote awareness of the new requirements

7.2 Seafarers

Seafarers are responsible for:

completing the module before the deadline

retaining their Verification of Training

producing evidence (digital format) when required

8. OneOcean access and completion process

8.1 Step-by-step process

The following step‑by‑step process describes how seafarers can access, complete and obtain verification for the ‘Prevention and Response to Violence & Harassment’ module (reference: 0900).

text:
The report, “Challenges and policy options to decarbonize the aviation and shipping sectors in California,” finds that there are currently no affordable, scalable low-GHG alternatives capable of replacing fossil fuels across these sectors. Over the longer term, the most promising options are ultra-low-carbon hydrogen-based fuels produced using renewable electricity.

However, these fuels remain at an early stage of development and are currently expensive to produce, meaning further technological advances and investment will be needed before they can be deployed at scale.

California already accounts for emissions from intrastate aviation and near-coastal maritime activity in its GHG inventory, but existing incentives and regulations do not directly target these sources. The report identifies this policy gap as an opportunity for the state to accelerate decarbonization in two of its most difficult-to-abate sectors while advancing its wider climate goals.

The analysis finds that current international, federal and state policies are unlikely to drive large-scale deployment of renewable hydrogen-based fuels in shipping and aviation. High capital and production costs, coupled with uncertainty over future demand and policy support, continue to hold back investment.

Revenue-certainty mechanisms, such as those being implemented in the United Kingdom, could offer a way forward, although California would need to carefully structure any such policy to avoid federal pre-emption.

As explained, the fuel pathway analysis points to hydrogen-derived e-fuels playing a far greater role than direct use of liquid hydrogen by 2045. Slow deployment of hydrogen-powered aircraft and the physical constraints of oceangoing vessels are expected to limit liquid hydrogen to a relatively small share of overall demand.

Hydrogen-derived fuels such as e-kerosene, e-diesel, e-methanol and e-ammonia, by contrast, could serve a much broader range of flights and voyages, with drop-in fuels potentially meeting almost all outbound aviation and maritime fuel demand.

The report also examines how a new Ultra-Low-Carbon Investment Standard (UCIS) could provide revenue certainty for California producers of ultra-low-carbon hydrogen-based fuels.

Under the proposed mechanism, providers of jet fuel and fuels used by oceangoing vessels, currently outside California’s Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) and Cap-and-Invest Program, would be required to purchase credits based on the greenhouse-gas intensity of their fuels, ICCT noted.

Furthermore, modeling suggests that a fixed credit price of $30 per tonne of CO₂ could create cost impacts comparable to existing greenhouse-gas mitigation charges on gasoline and diesel, while ensuring that the shipping and aviation sectors contribute to their own decarbonization.

More incremental policy measures could also help establish the foundations for longer-term progress. Explicitly including hydrogen-derived fuels in the 2027 Scoping Plan to Achieve Carbon Neutrality would help align state agencies around a common strategy for the two sectors, while redirecting state hydrogen funding toward shipping and aviation could support early pilot projects and infrastructure development.

title: Estonia Unveils Biomethane-Battery Powered Multipurpose State Vessel - Ship & Bunker
description:
Estonia has unveiled a new multipurpose state vessel powered primarily by biomethane and supported by battery-electric propulsion.
The 38 m Kratt was built by Estonian shipbuilder Baltic Workboats, Estonian State Fleet said in a LinkedIn post on Monday.
The Estonian State Fleet will use the vessel for buoy maintenance, fairway services, marine research, oil pollution response and search and rescue.
The vessel uses compressed biomethane as its primary fuel, with a 400 kWh battery system and four 350 kW gas generators.
The hull was built at Damen Shipyards Gdańsk and completed in 2025 before being transported to Estonia for outfitting and systems integration.
text:
Estonia has unveiled a new multipurpose state vessel powered primarily by biomethane and supported by battery-electric propulsion.

The 38 m Kratt was built by Estonian shipbuilder Baltic Workboats, Estonian State Fleet said in a LinkedIn post on Monday.

The Estonian State Fleet will use the vessel for buoy maintenance, fairway services, marine research, oil pollution response and search and rescue.

The vessel uses compressed biomethane as its primary fuel, with a 400 kWh battery system and four 350 kW gas generators.

It can travel up to 1,000 nautical miles at seven knots on biomethane and operate for up to two hours on battery power alone at five knots.

The batteries can provide power for up to 10 hours while at anchor.

The hull was built at Damen Shipyards Gdańsk and completed in 2025 before being transported to Estonia for outfitting and systems integration.

description:
تدركون جميعاً أن النقل البحري حافظ تاريخياً على مكانته كأكثر وسائل النقل الصديقة للبيئة للكميات الكبيرة من البضائع.
لقد بدأت بالفعل رحلة إزالة الكربون في النقل البحري.
وقد شرعت الدول الأعضاء في المنظمة البحرية الدولية بالفعل في مناقشات حول المزيد من التدابير التي من شأنها أن تمضي قدماً في مسار الشحن البحري نحو إزالة الكربون.
وقد أنشأت المنظمة البحرية الدولية منصة تعاون مع المؤسسات المالية لإزالة الحواجز التي قد تعيق الاستثمار في التحول إلى الطاقة في مجال النقل البحري.
كانت الصناعة شريكًا رئيسيًا مع المنظمة البحرية الدولية في رحلة إزالة الكربون من النقل البحري.
text:
الحفل الختامي

السبت 6 نوفمبر

جامعة ستراثكلايد، غلاسكو، المملكة المتحدة

كلمة كيتاك ليم، الأمين العام للمنظمة البحرية الدولية

أصحاب السعادة، السيدات والسادة,

يشرفني أن أخاطبكم في الحفل الختامي لهذا المؤتمر الهام.

وأود أن أعرب عن تقديري لهذه المبادرة الصناعية التي تجمع القادة على هامش مؤتمر الأطراف السادس والعشرين لمناقشة مستقبل صناعتنا الحيوية.

تدركون جميعاً أن النقل البحري حافظ تاريخياً على مكانته كأكثر وسائل النقل الصديقة للبيئة للكميات الكبيرة من البضائع.

ومع ذلك، ترسل أحدث التقارير المناخية رسالة واضحة. نحن بحاجة ماسة إلى تسريع عملية إزالة الكربون في جميع القطاعات الصناعية وقطاعات النقل.

كما يجب أن يؤدي النقل البحري دوره أيضاً.

لقد بدأت بالفعل رحلة إزالة الكربون في النقل البحري.

في أعقاب اتفاقية باريس، اعتمدت المنظمة البحرية الدولية في عام 2018 استراتيجية أولية لغازات الدفيئة تحدد رؤية والتزامًا بخفض انبعاثات غازات الدفيئة من النقل البحري الدولي على وجه السرعة.

اعتُمدت مجموعة شاملة من التدابير الإلزامية لتحسين كفاءة استخدام الطاقة في الأسطول العالمي بأكمله وتسريعها في يونيو من هذا العام، وستدخل حيز التنفيذ في العام المقبل.

وقد شرعت الدول الأعضاء في المنظمة البحرية الدولية بالفعل في مناقشات حول المزيد من التدابير التي من شأنها أن تمضي قدماً في مسار الشحن البحري نحو إزالة الكربون.

يجب علينا رفع مستوى طموحنا لمواكبة أحدث التطورات في المجتمع العالمي.

وقد طُرحت مقترحات لوضع حد أقصى للمحتوى الكربوني للوقود البحري بالاقتران مع آليات تسعير الكربون، استناداً إلى أدوات اقتصادية، أو تدابير قائمة على السوق.

ومع تعزيز العزم على التصدي لتغير المناخ، تؤكد المناقشات في مؤتمر الأطراف السادس والعشرين بوضوح على أن العمل المناخي يجب ألا يزيد من تعميق الفجوة بين البلدان المتقدمة والنامية.

ولدى المنظمة البحرية الدولية إطار عمل لتقييم ومعالجة الآثار المحتملة لتدابير الحد من غازات الدفيئة على الدول مع إيلاء اهتمام خاص لاحتياجات البلدان النامية، لا سيما الدول الجزرية الصغيرة النامية وأقل البلدان نمواً.

لجعل عملية إزالة الكربون من النقل البحري حقيقة واقعة، فإن الاستثمارات في الطاقة المتجددة والبنية التحتية للموانئ أمر بالغ الأهمية.

وقد أنشأت المنظمة البحرية الدولية منصة تعاون مع المؤسسات المالية لإزالة الحواجز التي قد تعيق الاستثمار في التحول إلى الطاقة في مجال النقل البحري.

كانت الصناعة شريكًا رئيسيًا مع المنظمة البحرية الدولية في رحلة إزالة الكربون من النقل البحري.

كما أن التعاون بين القطاعين العام والخاص له دور أساسي في مواصلة تطوير لوائح المنظمة البحرية الدولية وفي تسهيل البحث والتطوير والتعاون التكنولوجي.

لقد كانت دعوات قادة العالم للعمل، سواء من الحكومات أو من قطاع الأعمال، عالية وواضحة في الأسبوع الماضي في مؤتمر الأطراف السادس والعشرين.

علينا أن نتحرك الآن، وعلينا أن نتحرك بشكل عاجل، ولكننا نحتاج أيضًا إلى العمل بشكل تعاوني وشامل ومنصف ومستدام، دون أن نترك أحدًا يتخلف عن الركب.

أنا على يقين من أن الزخم الناتج عن الدورة السادسة والعشرين لمؤتمر الأطراف سيكون قوة دافعة للتقدم في المنظمة البحرية الدولية وسيبقي المجتمع البحري العالمي في قلب الجهود المبذولة لمكافحة تغير المناخ.

text:
Pacific Island countries have formalized a regional shipping pact, which is expected to deliver clean energy transition for the maritime industry across Oceania region.

The Pacific Blue Shipping Partnership (PBSP) was signed last week by seven Pacific transport ministers at a meeting in Majuro, Marshall Islands. The countries represented during the signing include Fiji, Federated States of Micronesia, Kiribati, Nauru, Marshall Islands, Tuvalu and Vanuatu. Palau and Tonga are also expected to sign the partnership.

For over a decade, the Pacific Island countries have been part of the 6PAC+ Alliance, mounting a high-ambition campaign at the International Maritime Organization(IMO) to phase out fossil fuel use in global shipping. While IMO member states continue to build consensus on global shipping emissions, the island nations said that the PBSP will help coordinate equitable transition in its region.

The ministers added that the PBSP is Pacific countries’ response to overhauling their domestic shipping, often described as a sector in crisis, trapped in a cycle of aged, poorly maintained ships servicing some of the longest, thinnest and highest cost domestic routes in the world.

Thus, PBSP seeks to re-orient climate funding for Pacific Island countries, with an aim to deliver a fleet of low-carbon vessels, climate resilient port infrastructure and skilled workers to ensure long-term maritime connectivity for the Island communities.

The PBSP Charter also established the organizational framework for the shipping partnership. The institution will oversee among other things funding mechanisms, governance and dispute resolution procedures, and the conditions for entry into force for the Charter. Marshall Islands capital Majuro was designated as the headquarters of the PBSP. The Marshallese transport minister was elected as the partnership’s inaugural Chair.

“The signing of the PBSP Charter transforms a shared vision into a permanent institution that will help drive the transition to cleaner, more resilient and more affordable maritime transport across our region,” said Hilton T. Kendall, Minister of Transportation for Marshall Islands.

Under the PBSP, the ministers agreed to make an application to the Green Climate Fund (GCF) to finance a demonstration fleet of wind-propelled vessels. Other targeted activities with GCF proposed funding include construction of maritime maintenance facilities, capacity building for seafarers and shoreside workers and institutional strengthening to kickstart the maritime transport transition.
